video.title: 7 Tips for an Effortless Serve ft. Giovanni Mpetshi-Perricard

classification.reason: The coach provides actionable cues and drills throughout the video, such as holding or pressing the non-dominant arm across the stomach, exaggerating throwing vectors to shape slice versus flat serves, and adopting specific visual tracking cues on return.

problem.title_as_question: How can you build an effortless, powerful, and accurate serve without elite height?
problem.definition: Recreational and non-giant players often struggle to generate effortless power and control because they misunderstand the serve as throwing directly toward the target or disconnect arm action from trunk and shoulder rotation.

quotes.text: In this video, we are going to go over seven things that Perkard does on his serve that you don't have to be 6'8 to copy.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Number one, the serve is a throw. And this is going to underpin our whole discussion.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you want your serve to feel effortless, the direction you want the ball to go does not match the direction that you throw your hand.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, the reason for this offset is that we are recruiting that internal shoulder rotation whip that we saw Jacob Deg Grom recruiting in the pitch.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And we have to feel this orthogonality in order to unlock those mechanics on the serve.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The serve is going to go down, but you're throwing your racket up. And the serve as a right-handed player is going to go to the left, but you're throwing your racket straight.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: See how he's throwing his racket at the net post? He's throwing his hand. He's throwing everything at the net post.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So a lot of times what I see from clients is their arm is back here, but the knees are still bent, the hips are still bent, they haven't actually started throwing yet
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The arm going back by itself unconnected to the throwing motion. That's where you start to lose a lot of velocity.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Pulls on the trunk to get that nice rotation early and then presses back across the stomach to help control that rotation late.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Hold the left shoulder. Hold it under your stomach as you serve. Pull and hold. Hold hold hold the left arm.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you are right eye dominant, you might actually be able to serve better overnight by adopting a more forward torso posture.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: By keeping your hips more forward like this, by stepping on the hidden side of your body, he's still got that coil and that stretch.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You just throw the hand back in a slightly different way so that when it gets to the top it cuts across the ball instead of slapping right through it.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Just figure out what happens here. Like exaggerate like whipping it around and slapping... and here, exaggerate throwing it this way.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Imagine an X in your trunk like this... connects one shoulder to the opposite hip... that stretches and contracts as you serve.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: In order to return really, really fast serves like this, watch the toss and watch your opponent's contact with a nice calm gaze.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You'll see it crystal clearly hit the ground. That's how you know you're doing it right.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: For the onehander, attach your arm to your trunk using your upper back.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: The serving arm rolls into external rotation and drops behind the head while the knees and hips remain fully bent before the upward drive begins.
Serve velocity drops significantly and the swing feels discombobulated and disconnected from the body.
Severe loss of serve directional accuracy when excessively coiling the torso away from the court.

causes.statement: The player attempts to throw the hand directly along the intended ball flight path rather than offset and upward to utilize internal shoulder rotation whip.
The hitting arm drops into external rotation behind the back statically before the lower body and trunk explosively initiate the upward throw.
The non-dominant arm fails to act as a counterbalance by pressing back across the stomach to brake trunk rotation late in the swing.
A pure-dextral server coils the torso too far away from the net, losing peripheral sight of the court with the rear dominant eye.

angles.summary: Internal shoulder rotation whip requires an angular offset between the hand throwing trajectory and the final ball flight line.
Roger Federer demonstrates launching the arm toward the net post on the ad side to maximize internal rotation whip.
The trunk acts as an abdominal X connecting each shoulder to the opposite hip that stretches during prep and contracts into contact.

solutions.summary: Hold or actively press the left arm back across your stomach during the finish to control trunk rotation.
Keep the hips and chest more forward and step on the hitting side to preserve dominant eye sightlines while coiling.
Exaggerate throwing the hand and racket either straight back for flat contact or outward behind the head for slice to feel the racket path differences.
solutions.external_goal: Throw racket trajectory outward to the net post or behind the head
